props.title: Children of the Corn II: The Final Sacrifice

sections.content: Children of the Corn II: The Final Sacrifice (1992) continues the supernatural horror franchise with a darker, more violent edge than its 1984 predecessor. Following the massacre in Gatlin, Nebraska, the surviving children are relocated to nearby Hemingford, setting up a familiar but evolved take on possessed youth horror. Like Village of the Damned (1960) and its 1995 remake, the film plays on deep-seated fears of corrupted innocence, though with distinctly American heartland imagery. The corn fields become more than just setting - they're practically characters, much like the oppressive forests in The Blair Witch Project (1999).

sections.content: Director David Price builds on Stephen King's original short story framework while taking the series in a more exploitation-horror direction. The film's emphasis on Native American mysticism and environmental themes distinguishes it from typical early 90s horror sequels like Hellraiser III (1992) or Candyman: Farewell to the Flesh (1995). The practical effects work, while dated, maintains the practical gore aesthetic that defined horror films of this era. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

While not as influential as the original Children of the Corn (1984), this sequel helped establish the template for rural horror that would later influence films like Jeepers Creepers (2001) and Signs (2002). The film's blend of religious fanaticism and supernatural horror echoes through later works like Red State (2011) and The Wicker Man (2006), though those films approached similar themes with more sophisticated execution.
